name: Brow tint kit
lead: A brow tint kit is a product containing a semi-permanent dye and an oxidizing developer that colours eyebrow hairs, and usually the skin beneath them, for several weeks. It is used to make pale, sparse or greying brows look darker and denser. Tints are offered as a salon or brow-bar service and as home kits. [1]

The kits are inexpensive and the effect is temporary. The main safety literature concerns contact allergy to hair-dye ingredients, particularly para-phenylenediamine (PPD) and related compounds, with case reports describing dermatitis and eye inflammation after eyelash and eyebrow dyeing. No controlled trials of home brow tint kits were identified. [2][3][4]

paras: A typical kit includes a tint cream or gel, a developer, a mixing dish and an applicator, with a barrier cream to limit skin staining. Professional and home procedures generally start with a patch test and cleansing, followed by application of the dye for a few minutes and removal with a damp pad. [1]

Reference sources describe results as lasting around three to six weeks on the hair, with skin staining fading sooner, depending on hair type, aftercare and product. Brands named in these sources include RefectoCil and Godefroy. [1]

Darkening the brows with pigments is long-standing: ancient Egyptians are described as using kohl, and henna and turmeric pastes are described in other cultures. Chemical tints are reported to have emerged in the early 20th century, and professional brow-tint services became widespread in salons from about the 1980s. [1] Social media trends such as the no-makeup look are said to have increased interest more recently. [1]

The dye deposits colour in the hair shaft and temporarily stains the skin. Oxidative hair dyes commonly rely on aromatic amines such as PPD, which are the main sensitizers described in the allergy literature. [3]

The product changes colour contrast on the hairs, making sparse or pale brows look more defined; this is described in reference works but has not been measured in controlled studies. The colour fades as dye wears off and hairs shed. [1]

A 2017 review of PPD allergy describes the compound as a frequent cause of allergic contact dermatitis and discusses diagnosis and management. [3] Case reports describe allergic dermatitis and periorbital swelling after permanent eyelash dye, and blepharoconjunctivitis from chloro-PPD contact allergy after eyelash colouring. [2][4]

Product instructions and clinicians commonly advise a patch test before use and caution that dye must not reach the eye. Home use has been described as carrying more risk of uneven results and staining than professional application. [1]

Tinting is discussed as a low-cost way to make light brows read as fuller, and the site rates the effect as strong but temporary. It is often paired with brow lamination or shaping in salon menus. [1]
No studies found that test brow tint kits for appearance outcomes. The related literature consists of case reports and reviews on allergic reactions to eyelash and hair dyes. [2][3][4]

timeline.event: Chemical tints reported to emerge as an alternative to kohl and henna. [1]
Dedicated professional brow-tint formulas spread in salons. [1]
